terms.definition: Cloud infrastructure owned by a third-party provider (AWS, Azure, GCP) and shared across multiple customers over the internet with pay-as-you-go pricing.
terms.example: Hosting a startup website on AWS EC2 — you rent virtual servers without owning any hardware.

terms.definition: Cloud infrastructure used exclusively by a single organization — hosted in their own data center or by a provider, but not shared with other customers.
terms.example: A bank running VMware or OpenStack in its own data center to provide cloud-like services only to internal teams.

terms.definition: A combination of public and private cloud environments, allowing data and applications to move between them based on compliance, cost, or performance needs.
terms.example: A hospital keeps patient records in its private cloud (HIPAA compliance) but runs its booking website on AWS.

terms.definition: Cloud infrastructure shared among organizations with similar concerns — such as common compliance requirements, security policies, or mission objectives.
terms.example: Universities sharing a research computing cloud, or government agencies sharing a classified cloud environment.

terms.definition: Infrastructure as a Service — the cloud provides raw infrastructure (servers, storage, networking). The customer manages the OS, middleware, runtime, applications, and data.
terms.example: Amazon EC2 (virtual servers), Amazon S3 (raw storage). You choose the OS, you patch it, you manage it.

terms.definition: Platform as a Service — the cloud provides infrastructure plus a runtime platform. Developers deploy only their application code and data without managing servers or OS.
terms.example: AWS Elastic Beanstalk — upload your code and AWS handles deployment, scaling, load balancing, and OS patches.

terms.definition: Software as a Service — fully managed applications delivered over the internet. Users only use the software; the provider manages everything including hardware, OS, application, and updates.
terms.example: Gmail, Zoom, Salesforce. You open the app and use it — no server management required.

terms.definition: The AWS framework defining what AWS secures ('of the cloud' — physical hardware, networking, data centers) vs. what the customer secures ('in the cloud' — data, IAM, OS patches, application code).
terms.example: AWS secures the physical EC2 host. The customer secures the OS password, application firewall rules, and data encryption settings.

terms.definition: Technology that allows multiple virtual machines to run on a single physical server by abstracting hardware resources through software called a hypervisor.
terms.example: 1 physical AWS server hosts 20 EC2 instances simultaneously — each customer gets an isolated virtual machine.

terms.definition: Software layer between physical hardware and virtual machines that allocates CPU, RAM, and storage to each VM and enforces isolation between them.
terms.example: VMware ESXi, Microsoft Hyper-V, KVM, Xen, and AWS Nitro are all hypervisors.

terms.definition: A bare-metal hypervisor that runs directly on physical hardware without requiring a host operating system. Faster and more efficient — used in production environments and cloud data centers.
terms.example: AWS Nitro, VMware ESXi, Microsoft Hyper-V (bare-metal mode). Used in all major cloud provider data centers.

terms.definition: A hosted hypervisor that runs on top of an existing operating system. Slower due to the extra OS layer — used primarily for development and testing on personal computers.
terms.example: VirtualBox, VMware Workstation running on a Windows or macOS laptop.

terms.definition: A software emulation of a complete computer with its own OS, applications, and virtual hardware (CPU, RAM, disk), sharing the underlying physical hardware with other VMs via a hypervisor.
terms.example: An EC2 t2.micro instance — a virtual machine with 1 vCPU and 1GB RAM, sharing physical hardware with other customer instances.

terms.definition: AWS's custom Type 1 bare-metal hypervisor that offloads virtualization functions to dedicated Nitro hardware cards, enabling near bare-metal performance and reducing security attack surface.
terms.example: When you launch an EC2 instance, the Nitro System manages isolation, networking, and storage without consuming customer CPU cycles.

terms.definition: The ability of multiple customers to share the same physical infrastructure while remaining logically isolated from one another — made possible by virtualization.
terms.example: Thousands of AWS customers run EC2 instances on the same physical servers, yet no customer can see or access another's data.

terms.definition: A virtualization disadvantage where multiple VMs compete for the same physical CPU, RAM, or disk resources, causing performance degradation. Also called the 'noisy neighbor' problem.
terms.example: If 20 VMs all run CPU-intensive tasks simultaneously on the same host, each VM's performance degrades because they compete for the same physical cores.

terms.definition: A rare but serious security vulnerability where an attacker exploits a flaw in the hypervisor to break out of one VM and gain unauthorized access to another VM or the host.
terms.example: A theoretical attack where a malicious EC2 customer exploits a hypervisor bug to read memory from another customer's VM on the same host.

terms.definition: A point-in-time copy of a virtual machine's complete state — OS, data, configuration — that enables fast backup and restoration.
terms.example: An AWS AMI (Amazon Machine Image) is a snapshot of an EC2 instance that can be used to launch identical copies or restore a previous state.

terms.definition: The most common type of virtualization — running multiple virtual machines on a single physical server. Each VM has its own OS and applications.
terms.example: Amazon EC2 — multiple customer instances running on the same AWS physical server hardware.

terms.definition: Creating virtual networks on top of shared physical network hardware using software, allowing isolated private networks to operate independently.
terms.example: Amazon VPC — each customer gets their own isolated virtual network within AWS's physical network infrastructure.

terms.definition: Capital Expenditure (CapEx) is upfront hardware investment — the data center model. Operational Expenditure (OpEx) is ongoing pay-as-you-go spending — the cloud model.
terms.example: A company that builds its own data center pays CapEx. A company using AWS pays OpEx — monthly based on usage, no upfront hardware cost.

terms.definition: A pre-configured template for launching EC2 instances — includes OS, installed software, and configuration. The cloud equivalent of a VM snapshot or template.
terms.example: Amazon Linux 2023 AMI — a ready-made template that launches an EC2 instance with Amazon Linux pre-installed.
